questions.text: List the **four** methods of system implementation.

scheme.mark_scheme: Direct, parallel, pilot, phased. All four (2); two or three (1)

questions.title: System implementation
questions.text: Describe what happens during the **implementation** stage of the system life cycle.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): new system installed (hardware / software); data transferred / converted from the old system; users trained; changeover method used to replace the old system
scheme.model_answer: The new system is installed, data is transferred from the old system, users are trained and the old system is replaced using a changeover method.

questions.title: Direct: advantage and disadvantage
questions.text: State **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of **direct** changeover.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Advantage (1): fastest; cheapest; benefits immediately; no double work
Disadvantage (1): very risky; no backup if it fails; data loss; all staff must be trained before
scheme.model_answer: Advantage: it is the fastest method. Disadvantage: it is very risky because there is no backup system.

questions.title: Parallel: advantage and disadvantage
questions.text: State **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of **parallel** running.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Advantage (1): old system available as a backup; more secure; results can be compared; gradual training
Disadvantage (1): expensive; double workload / data entered twice; takes longer
scheme.model_answer: Advantage: the old system is still available as a backup. Disadvantage: staff have to enter all data twice.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Pilot: the whole system is introduced in one part / department / branch first (1)
- Phased: the system is introduced one module / function at a time across the whole organisation (1)
scheme.model_answer: In pilot implementation one department uses the complete new system first, whereas in phased implementation everybody starts using the system one part at a time.

questions.title: Which method
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the method described.

prefill: The safest method, but the most expensive
The fastest and cheapest, but the most risky
One branch of a bank uses the new system before the others
The accounts module is introduced first, then stock control, then payroll

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Parallel (1); 2 Direct (1); 3 Pilot (1); 4 Phased (1)

questions.title: A seaport system
questions.text: Suggest an implementation method: *A system that tracks the arrival of cargo ships at the seaport is being replaced.*

scheme.mark_scheme: Parallel (1)

questions.text: Suggest an implementation method: *A café is introducing a system that allows customers to complete their orders electronically instead of ordering from the staff. The management wants the change to happen quickly and cheaply.*

scheme.mark_scheme: Direct (1)

questions.title: A school's clubs
questions.text: Suggest an implementation method: *A school introduces a new system for managing hobby clubs. The old system is a paper log. The new system is first used by one grade, and later by the whole school.*

scheme.mark_scheme: Pilot (1)

questions.title: The safest method
questions.text: Direct changeover is the safest method because the new system is used by everyone immediately.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Direct changeover is the riskiest; parallel running is the safest because the old system remains as a backup.

questions.title: Phased implementation
questions.text: For which system is **phased** implementation most suitable?

options.content: A small shop's single till program
A hospital system with separate modules for patients, prescriptions and billing
A new organisation with no old system
A system that must be compared with the old one for a month

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: Phased implementation suits large systems that can be divided into independent modules.

questions.title: Implementation at a clinic
questions.text: A clinic is replacing its paper patient records with a computer system. Choose **one** type of system implementation that could be used by the clinic, and write one advantage and one disadvantage of the method you have chosen.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Method: direct or parallel (1). Do not accept pilot or phased.
Direct — advantage: fastest / cheapest (1); disadvantage: very risky / no backup (1)
Parallel — advantage: old system available as backup / more secure (1); disadvantage: expensive / double work (1)
scheme.model_answer: Parallel. Advantage: the paper records are still available if the new system fails. Disadvantage: staff must record every patient twice, which takes extra time.

questions.title: A supermarket chain
questions.text:
A supermarket chain with 40 shops across Kazakhstan is replacing its stock-control system. All shops sell the same products and use the same procedures.

Discuss which implementation method is most suitable. Refer to at least two methods.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Up to 4 marks:
- Pilot is suitable: test in one shop first, problems found before rolling out to 40 shops; shops are similar so results apply (2)
- Direct for all 40 is too risky — failure would stop all shops (1)
- Parallel in 40 shops would be very expensive / double work (1)
- Justified conclusion (1)
[Max 4]
scheme.model_answer: A pilot implementation is best: the new system can be used in one shop first, so problems are found and fixed while only one shop is affected, and because all shops work the same way the results will apply to the others. Direct changeover in all 40 shops at once would be too risky, because one fault could stop every shop, and parallel running in 40 shops would double the staff's work and cost a lot. So the chain should pilot the system and then roll it out.

questions.title: Evaluate the methods
questions.text: A national bank is replacing the software that processes all customer payments. Evaluate the four methods of system implementation for the bank and recommend one.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Each method evaluated with an advantage / disadvantage linked to the bank (max 4): direct — fast / cheap but failure would stop all payments; parallel — safe, results compared, but expensive / double work; pilot — one branch first, limited risk, but payments link all branches; phased — one function at a time, but slow / interfaces
Recommendation (1) with justification (1): parallel (or pilot) because payments are critical
scheme.model_answer: Direct changeover is the fastest and cheapest, but if the new software failed, no customer could make payments, which is unacceptable for a bank. Parallel running is the safest: both systems process payments and the results are compared, but it is expensive and doubles the work. A pilot in one branch limits the risk, but payments pass between all branches, so it is hard to isolate one. Phased introduction of functions one at a time spreads the risk but is slow. I recommend parallel running, because payment processing is critical and errors could cost customers money.

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Parallel (1); 2 Pilot (1); 3 Direct (1)

parts.title: Clinic
parts.text: A clinic is introducing an electronic appointment system. Choose one type of system implementation that could be used by the clinic and write one advantage and one disadvantage of it.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Direct or parallel (1). Do not accept pilot and phased.
Direct: advantage fastest (1); disadvantage very risky (1)
Parallel: advantage old system as backup / more secure (1); disadvantage expensive / double work (1)
scheme.model_answer: Parallel. Advantage: the old appointment book can still be used if the new system fails. Disadvantage: receptionists must record every appointment twice.

scheme.mark_scheme: Pilot: whole system in one part first (1); phased: one part of the system at a time everywhere (1)
scheme.model_answer: Pilot gives the whole system to one department first, whereas phased gives everyone one module at a time.

questions.title: A national retail chain
questions.text: An electronics retailer with 60 shops is introducing a new system that handles sales, stock, staff rotas and customer loyalty cards.

parts.title: Discuss
parts.text: Discuss whether pilot or phased implementation would be more suitable for the retailer.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Up to 4 marks:
- Pilot: one shop tests all functions; problems affect only one shop; shops are similar (1–2)
- Phased: modules (sales, stock, rotas, loyalty) introduced one at a time in all shops; staff learn gradually; one module failure only (1–2)
- Drawbacks of each (slow; interfaces; pilot shop not typical) (1)
- Justified conclusion (1)
scheme.model_answer: With a pilot, one shop would use the complete system first, so any problem would affect only that shop, and because the shops are similar the lessons would apply to all 60. With phased implementation the four modules would be introduced one by one in every shop, so staff learn gradually, but it would take a long time and the old and new modules must work together. A pilot is better, because the shops are identical and the full system can be proven in one place before the rollout.

prefill: Staff must enter every sale into two systems
If the new system fails on the first day, no shop can sell anything
The loyalty-card module is introduced three months after the sales module
Only the Almaty shop uses the new system in its first month

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Parallel (1); 2 Direct (1); 3 Phased (1); 4 Pilot (1)

summary: The four methods of implementing (changing over to) a new system — direct, parallel, pilot and phased — how each works, their advantages and disadvantages, and how to choose the right method for a scenario.

blocks.content: The stage of the system life cycle in which the **new system is installed and put into use**, replacing the **old system**. It includes installing hardware and software, **transferring (converting) data** from the old system, **training users** and choosing a **changeover method**.
There are **four** implementation methods. They differ in **how quickly** the old system is replaced and **how much risk** the organisation takes if the new system fails.

Direct    old ███████████|░░░░░░░░░░░░░  new    the old system stops one day, the new one starts the next
Parallel  old ███████████████████████|          both systems run together for a period
          new        ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░
Pilot     dept A   ███|░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░       one department / branch tries it first,
          dept B   ██████████|░░░░░░░░░░       then everyone changes
Phased    module 1 ███|░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░       the system is introduced part by part
          module 2 ███████|░░░░░░░░░░░░░░
          module 3 ███████████|░░░░░░░░░░
blocks.caption: The four implementation methods (old system = ███, new system = ░░░)

blocks.content: The old system is **stopped completely** and the new system is **started immediately** in its place — on a fixed date ("big bang").

blocks.title: Direct changeover
rows: **Fastest** method — benefits of the new system immediately
**Very risky** — if the new system fails there is **no backup** system to fall back on
**Cheapest** — only one system is run, no duplicate work
Data may be **lost** if the new system has errors
Staff do not have to use two systems
**All staff** must be trained before the changeover date
Problems affect the **whole organisation** at once

blocks.title: When direct changeover is suitable
blocks.content:
- A **café** introduces electronic ordering instead of ordering from staff — small, simple system; a short failure is not dangerous.
- The old system **no longer works** or is completely different, so running both is impossible.
- A **new organisation** with no old system.

The **old and new systems run at the same time** for a period. The same data is entered into both and the **results are compared**. When the new system is shown to be reliable, the old one is stopped.

blocks.title: Parallel running
rows: **Safest** — the old system is a **backup** if the new one fails
**Most expensive** — two systems, more staff time
Results of the new system can be **checked** against the old one
**Double workload** — data entered twice; staff may be overworked
Staff can be **trained gradually** while the old system still works
Staff may keep relying on the old system

blocks.title: When parallel running is suitable
blocks.content:
- **Critical** systems where failure is unacceptable: a **seaport** tracking cargo ships, **hospital / clinic** records, **banking**, **payroll**.
- When the new system's results must be **checked against** the old one.
The **whole new system** is introduced in **one part of the organisation first** — one department, branch, shop or class. When it works well there, it is introduced in all the other parts.

blocks.title: Pilot implementation
rows: If the system fails, **only one part** of the organisation is affected
Takes **longer** than direct changeover before everyone uses the system
Errors are found and fixed **before** the full rollout
The pilot site may not be **typical** of the others
Staff in the pilot can **train** other staff later
Two systems exist in the organisation at the same time
Cheaper and less risky than parallel for the whole organisation
If the pilot fails, that department is still badly affected

blocks.title: When pilot implementation is suitable
blocks.content:
- A **supermarket chain** tries a new checkout system in **one shop**.
- A **school** introduces a new club-management system for **one grade** before the whole school.
- A bank tests new software in **one branch**.
The new system is introduced **gradually, one part (module / function) at a time**, across the whole organisation. Each phase is introduced only when the previous one works.

blocks.title: Phased implementation
rows: If one module fails, only **that part** of the system is affected
**Slowest** method — the full system is in use only after all phases
Staff learn the system **gradually**, one part at a time
Old and new parts must **work together** (interfaces), which can be complex
Errors in each phase are fixed before the next
Benefits of the full system arrive late

blocks.title: When phased implementation is suitable
blocks.content:
- A large **ERP** system: first **accounts**, then **stock control**, then **payroll**.
- A school system: first **attendance**, then **marks**, then **reports to parents**.
- A system that can be divided into **independent modules**.

blocks.title: The four methods compared
rows: Risk if the new system fails
Small, simple or non-critical systems; old system unusable

blocks.title: How to choose a method for a scenario
items: How **critical** is the system? If failure is dangerous or very costly → **parallel**.
Does the organisation have **several similar sites** (shops, branches, classes)? → **pilot**.
Can the system be split into **independent parts**? → **phased**.
Is it **small**, cheap, urgent, or is the old system **unusable**? → **direct**.
Always **justify** the choice with details from the scenario, and mention the trade-off (cost, time, risk).

blocks.title: Choose the method (exam style)
blocks.content:
| Situation | Method | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| A system that tracks the arrival of cargo ships at the seaport is being replaced | **Parallel** | Critical; errors could cause accidents or losses, so the old system is kept as a backup |
| A school introduces a new system for managing hobby clubs, first for one group of students | **Pilot** | Tested on part of the school before all students use it |
| A café lets customers order electronically instead of ordering from staff | **Direct** | Small, simple and not critical; quick and cheap |
| A city hospital replaces patient records, prescriptions and billing over a year | **Phased** | Large system with separate modules introduced one at a time |

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: List the four methods of system implementation. [2]**
**Direct**, **parallel**, **pilot**, **phased** (any two for 1 mark, all four for 2).

**Q: Choose one type of system implementation that could be used by the clinic, and give one advantage and one disadvantage. [3]**
**Parallel** (1). Advantage: the **old system is available as a backup** / results can be compared (1). Disadvantage: **expensive** and **double work** for staff (1).
*(Or **direct**: advantage — fastest / cheapest; disadvantage — very risky, no backup.)*

**Q: Compare pilot and phased implementation. [2]**
Pilot introduces the **whole system in one part of the organisation** first (1), **whereas** phased introduces the system **one module at a time** across the **whole organisation** (1).

- Confusing **pilot** (one **location** gets the **whole** system) with **phased** (everyone gets **one part** at a time).
- Saying parallel running is "fast" — it is the **slowest and most expensive**, but the **safest**.
- Choosing a method without **linking** the reason to the scenario.
- Forgetting **data conversion** and **training**, which are needed with every method.

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: Describe each of the four implementation methods.
Give two advantages and two disadvantages of each.
Which method is the safest? The fastest? The cheapest?
What is the difference between pilot and phased implementation?
Choose and justify a method for: a new airline booking system; a new library system in one school of a network of 20 schools; a new online menu for a small café.
